title: Strasburg Road subdivision near Huron Natural Area approved
subtitle: Woodhaven Road rezoning, road salt advocacy, 2026 calendar, gas research agreement and demolition approvals also decided.
overview: Council gave draft approval to an industrial subdivision at 1700 Strasburg Road and McBrine Drive, next to the Huron Natural Area {{vote:m3}}. Many delegates opposed it, citing consultation with Six Nations of the Grand River, wetland loss and buffers. Staff and supporters said the land is already zoned industrial, and the subdivision brings land dedications and further studies. Council also approved a rezoning at 137 Woodhaven Road {{vote:m1}}, despite concern for the current tenants.

Council asked the Province to limit liability for property owners and contractors who follow salt best practices, with the aim of reducing road salt use {{vote:m14}}. It approved a University of Waterloo gas infrastructure research agreement, next steps for the Enabling 4 Units program, and the 2026 meeting calendar, which includes a possible November 9, 2026 meeting.

After a closed session, Council directed staff to proceed with land acquisition negotiations for the City Park Strategy. The meeting opened with Remembrance Day remarks about a new veterans crosswalk at the Kitchener Memorial Auditorium. Staff also received national awards for parking service and the downtown cycling grid.

decisions.item: 1700 Strasburg Road draft plan of subdivision
decisions.detail: Council granted draft approval to the industrial subdivision with conditions, authorized a subdivision agreement and endorsed the updated urban design brief {{vote:m3}}.
Council approved the zoning change for 137 Woodhaven Road as recommended in staff report DSD-2025-370.
Council urged the Province and Attorney General to adopt limited occupier liability legislation tied to provincial salt best practices, and to develop standard contractor training and practices.

Council approved the calendar as amended, allowing a possible Council meeting on November 9, 2026, extra planning committee meetings where legislated timelines require, and rescheduling by resolution.
Council approved a sponsored research agreement with the University of Waterloo and authorized the General Manager of Infrastructure Services to sign it.
Council endorsed the next steps for the Enabling 4 Units program as outlined in staff report DSD-2025-411.
Council directed staff to proceed with land acquisition negotiations as discussed in closed session and authorized an acknowledgment letter to the property owner.
Council approved a heritage permit to demolish the picnic shelter, on condition that Heritage Planning staff review the final drawings before a demolition permit is issued.

debate: Delegates opposing the Strasburg Road plan asked for deferral. They said the Six Nations of the Grand River recommendations on wetland compensation, buffers and tree planting were not adopted, and that consultation was inadequate.

Delegates raised environmental concerns. These included the loss of four small wetlands replaced by one larger constructed wetland, wetland buffer size, the effect on turtle nesting and grassland bird habitat, road salt runoff, and the lack of a cumulative impact study. Some also asked why industrial space was needed when vacant industrial buildings exist.

Staff said the land is privately owned and already zoned for employment uses, so the owner could build on one large lot through site plan approval with no public process. Subdivision allows land to be conveyed to the City, with 34 pages of conditions, further environmental studies and continued Six Nations review. Appeals to the Ontario Land Tribunal are limited to prescribed parties.

Supporting councillors said the subdivision gave better protection than development of the whole site would, and that the land was sold years ago. One councillor opposed it, citing the unresolved Six Nations recommendations and the applicant's unwillingness to widen the wetland buffer. Council ended debate and voted.

On Woodhaven Road, some councillors opposed the rezoning because of tenant displacement and the owner's limited compensation. Others said those concerns are not planning grounds, an appeal to the Ontario Land Tribunal could cost the City, and the owner's commitments to return tenants at the same rent improved the proposal.
